name: MACS lift

card.summary: A short-scar facelift that hangs the lower and mid face from above with purse-string sutures along a purely vertical vector; surgeon series report quicker recovery.
card.note: Evidence is mostly from the surgeons who developed and promote it; limits are discussed for the lower face and neck.

quick.overview:
The MACS (minimal access cranial suspension) lift is a short-scar facelift that uses a short incision in front of the ear and suspends sagging tissue upward with permanent purse-string sutures anchored to firm tissue above. It was proposed in 2002 as a modification of the S-lift.

Its developers report operating times of about 2 to 2.5 hours under local anesthesia and a quicker recovery than classic facelifts, with results they describe as comparably stable. Independent reviews have discussed advantages and limitations.
quick.mechanism: Purse-string sutures lift the neck and lower face along a vertical vector with no lateral tension; an optional third, malar suture adds midface correction in the extended version.
quick.risks: Wikipedia says less skin is raised, so bleeding and nerve-injury risk are lower than with traditional facelifts, but general facelift risks still apply, including hematoma, scarring and nerve injury. Reviews have outlined limitations for the lower third of the face.

lead: The minimal access cranial suspension (MACS) lift is a short-scar rhytidectomy for the lower and middle third of the face that uses a vertical vector, involves no lateral tension, and in its authors' description can be performed under local anesthesia in 2 to 2.5 hours.[1] It was proposed in 2002 as a modified version of the S-lift, suspending tissue with purse-string sutures.[2]

Wikipedia states that the MACS lift uses a short incision in front of the ear and suspends sagging tissue vertically from above, raises less skin so bleeding and nerve injury risk is lower, takes about 2.5 hours against 3.5 for a traditional facelift, and has a recovery of 2 to 3 weeks versus 3 to 4.[3] The developers write that it reduces recovery time and morbidity and that results are as stable as more classic, extended techniques.[1]

It exists in a simple version with two purse-string sutures for the neck and lower face and an extended version that adds a third, malar suture for the midface.[4] The literature is dominated by surgeons who use the technique; independent assessments exist, including one examining its advantages and limitations.[5]
infobox: Local possible; 2 to 2.5 hours per authors[1]

paras: The technique uses permanent purse-string sutures placed through a short temporal-preauricular incision and anchored to deep temporal fascia, lifting the tissues vertically.[2][4] Surgeons have proposed ways to optimise results[6] and a deep-plane hybrid, the minimal access deep plane extended (MADE) vertical facelift, that combines features of deep-plane and short-incision lifts.[7]

A 2008 article examined indications and limitations of the MACS lift for the lower third of the face.[8] A later review discussed its advantages and limitations for facial rejuvenation.[5] The technique has also been used to treat complications of APTOS thread lifting, together with fat grafting.[9]

As with other facelifts, risks include hematoma, nerve injury, skin necrosis, scarring and anesthesia reactions; Wikipedia states that short-incision methods carry lower bleeding and nerve-injury risk because less skin is raised.[3]

Studies are mostly surgeon-reported series. The 2007 paper describes the procedure and reports stability comparable to extended techniques in the authors' view.[1] A 2014 retrospective analysis compared platelet-rich plasma with fat grafting, with and without MACS lift, on recovery time and aesthetic outcome.[10] A 2018 study examined how facelift practice evolved with new techniques.[11] No randomized comparisons with other facelifts were found.

timeline.event: S-lift described; later basis for MACS.[2]
MACS lift proposed as a modified S-lift.[2]
Short-scar rhytidectomy and third malar suture papers published.[1][4]
MADE vertical facelift described as a hybrid technique.[7]
